items.title: Gutenberg's actual innovation
items.claim: Movable type existed in East Asia centuries before Gutenberg. What was his specific contribution in the 1450s?

options.text: Combining a metal-alloy movable type, oil-based ink, and an adapted screw press into a single workflow

items.reveal_title: An integrated system, not a single component
items.reveal:
Bi Sheng's clay movable type dates to around 1040 in Song China; Korean metal type predates Gutenberg. Gutenberg's system combined durable type, oil-based ink and a press into commercially viable output.

Eisenstein's The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) remains a key source.
items.why: Many famous 'inventions' are integrations of pre-existing components into a new workflow.

items.title: The penny press in the US
items.claim: The first US penny press paper, the New York Sun, launched in which year and at what price compared to existing dailies?

options.text: 1833, at one cent versus typical six cents

items.reveal:
Benjamin Day's New York Sun used steam printing, street vendors and advertising-funded distribution.

The model transformed expectations of who newspapers were for.
items.why: Pricing innovations can democratise media access as much as technology can.

items.title: The 1938 War of the Worlds 'panic'
items.claim: Orson Welles's 1938 radio broadcast is famed for causing mass panic. What does later research say about the audience reaction?

options.text: Audience numbers were modest and the panic was likely exaggerated by newspapers competing with radio

items.reveal:
Pooley and Socolow (2013, Slate) reviewed contemporaneous ratings and surveys, concluding the audience was much smaller than later legend implied and significant panic was uncommon.

The story remains a staple in media-effects discussions.
items.why: Media history is itself shaped by competing media industries telling stories about each other.

items.title: UK colour TV adoption
items.claim: BBC2 began regular colour transmissions in 1967. Roughly how many years until colour TV licences in the UK overtook black-and-white?
items.reveal:
Colour licences overtook black-and-white in the UK in 1976. The technology's price had fallen and rentals were widespread.

The BBC issued the last analogue black-and-white licences as a category in 2020 (around 6,000 remained).
items.why: Technology adoption follows distinctive S-curves shaped by cost and infrastructure.

items.title: Facebook user growth
items.claim: Facebook launched in February 2004. About how many years to reach 1 billion monthly active users?
items.reveal:
Facebook hit 1 billion monthly active users in October 2012. WhatsApp, Instagram and Messenger (all Meta-owned) each later reached similar scale.

TikTok reached around 1 billion users in about 5 years from its 2016 launch.
items.why: Platform growth has accelerated through successive generations of social products.

items.title: Cultivation theory
items.claim: George Gerbner's cultivation analysis (from 1960s onwards) argued heavy television viewers develop what tendency?

options.text: A 'mean world' perception, overestimating crime risk and danger

items.reveal_title: Heavy viewers perceive the world as more dangerous
items.reveal:
Gerbner and Gross (1976) argued long-term exposure to violent television cultivates beliefs aligned with TV's symbolic world, including overestimation of crime victimisation risk.

Later meta-analyses (Shanahan and Morgan, 1999) found small but consistent effects.
items.why: Long-running exposure can shape perception of social reality in measurable ways.

items.title: Agenda-setting's 1968 study
items.claim: McCombs and Shaw's 1968 Chapel Hill study compared issue rankings in news media to issue rankings by which group?
items.reveal_title: Undecided voters' priorities tracked news coverage
items.reveal:
McCombs and Shaw (1972 publication of 1968 fieldwork) showed close correlation between news coverage of campaign issues and what undecided voters considered important.

The finding inspired decades of research distinguishing 'first-level' (issue) and 'second-level' (attribute) agenda-setting.
items.why: Media may not tell us what to think, but they shape what we think about.

items.title: Filter bubble evidence
items.claim: Eli Pariser popularised 'filter bubble' in 2011. What does subsequent empirical research generally find about algorithmic news exposure?

options.text: Strong evidence of total ideological isolation
Modest effects on average; heavy partisans self-select more than algorithms force them
No relationship between algorithms and exposure
Algorithms always expose users to all viewpoints equally

items.reveal:
Studies including Bakshy et al. (2015, Science) on Facebook and Guess et al. (2023, Nature) on Facebook/Instagram found algorithmic effects were measurable but typically smaller than user-choice effects.

The area remains actively debated and methodologically complex.
items.why: Strong popular claims about media often require nuanced empirical revisions.

items.title: Netflix's product transitions
items.claim: Netflix shipped its first DVD in 1998. When did it launch streaming and stop adding new DVD subscribers?

options.text: Streaming launched 2007; DVD service ended in 2023

items.reveal:
Streaming launched in 2007 as a bundled feature; it later overtook the DVD business by revenue. Netflix shipped its final DVD on 29 September 2023.

The business is sometimes cited as a case of successful cannibalisation of one's own product.
items.why: Strategic transitions can run two business models in parallel for years.

items.title: When 'deepfake' entered usage
items.claim: The term 'deepfake' originated where and when?

options.text: A Reddit user's username in late 2017

items.reveal_title: A Reddit username, then a community, then a term
items.reveal:
The label spread from a Reddit user 'deepfakes' in late 2017 to wider use within months.

Generative adversarial network methods underlying the technique date to Goodfellow et al. (2014).
items.why: Names for new media practices often emerge from online communities, not laboratories.

items.title: The Leveson Inquiry
items.claim: The Leveson Inquiry (2011-2012) examined UK press conduct and ethics following which trigger?

options.text: The 2011 phone-hacking revelations at the News of the World

items.reveal_title: Phone hacking led to a public inquiry
items.reveal:
The inquiry's 2012 report proposed a new statutory underpinning for press self-regulation; debate over implementation continued for years.

IPSO replaced the Press Complaints Commission in 2014.
items.why: Regulatory frameworks are often reformed only after very public scandals.

items.title: Public service broadcasting funding
items.claim: The UK TV licence fee predates the BBC's television service. When was a wireless (radio) licence first introduced in the UK?
items.reveal_title: 1922, the same year the BBC formed
items.reveal:
The Wireless Telegraphy Act framework underlay radio licences from 1922. A combined radio-television licence followed in 1946; colour licences from 1968.

The model has been debated and reviewed multiple times since the 2000s.
items.why: Funding models for public service broadcasting are political settlements that periodically come under review.
